content_voiceover: S F 3 B 1 mutations are usually considered favorable in M D S, but this slide shows that's not the whole story, outcomes actually split into three distinct categories depending on co-mutation pattern. S F 3 B 1 with the 5 q signature makes up about seven percent of S F 3 B 1 mutant cases. S F 3 B 1 beta, about fifteen percent, occurs alongside B C O R, B C O R L 1, N RAS, R U N X 1, S R S F 2, or S T A G 2, and these co-mutations erase the favorable effect, tracking closely with wild type or even worse outcomes on both leukemia free and overall survival curves. The remaining seventy eight percent, S F 3 B 1 alpha, meaning S F 3 B 1 mutated without those adverse partners, shows the classically favorable, prolonged survival curve well above wild type. The Kaplan Meier curves show hazard ratios around three for S F 3 B 1 beta compared to alpha, both for leukemia free and overall survival, all highly significant.
keypoints: SF3B1 5q variant: about 7 percent of SF3B1-mutant cases
SF3B1 beta, about 15 percent, co-mutated with BCOR, BCORL1, NRAS, RUNX1, SRSF2, or STAG2, loses favorable prognosis
SF3B1 alpha, about 78 percent, retains the classic favorable outcome
Co-mutation pattern, not SF3B1 status alone, determines prognosis
Hazard ratio around 3 for beta versus alpha in both LFS and OS
keypoint_voiceover: Key exam point, S F 3 B 1 is not uniformly good prognosis, the co-mutation pattern matters. S F 3 B 1 alpha, the majority without adverse partners, keeps the favorable course, but S F 3 B 1 beta with B C O R, R U N X 1, N RAS, S R S F 2 or S T A G 2 behaves like a high risk clone despite the S F 3 B 1 mutation.
